That includes a window that cannot be fetched or is invalid, a pin outside the window, an app that pins more than one version, a C++ repository with no pin, a packaged Python repository with no published runtime among its versions, an invalid primary-version, and a missing or invalid vergil.toml. It also fails when vrg-ci-resolve is not on PATH (a [dependencies].vergil pin older than vergil-tooling 2.1.253). There is no fallback. A resolver stderr line starting warning: becomes a ::warning:: annotation and does not fail the job (the resolver prints none today).

The install, the pin reading and the derivation live in install-tooling.sh, read-pin.sh and derive.sh rather than inline YAML so they can be unit tested; see tests/install-tooling.test.sh, which runs every install path against stubbed git, curl and uv (and apt, gpg and sudo stubs that must never be called), and actions/shared/setup/vergil/tests/derive.test.sh, which runs the real resolver against the fixture window in tests/fixtures/window.json (one case stubs the resolver to test the warning: passthrough), and tests/read-pin.test.sh. The smoke-setup-vergil workflow runs those tests and checks the action's outputs end to end.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
The action and the resolver read these parts of the consuming repository's vergil.toml:

[project]
repository-type = "library"   # library: the whole window; otherwise one version
primary-language = "python"

[dependencies]
vergil = "v2.1"               # vergil-tooling tag to install, and window ref

[ci]
# versions = ["3.14"]         # optional pin inside the window; one entry for an app
# primary-version = "3.13"    # optional; defaults to the newest resolved version

Leave [ci].versions out so the repository follows the window. Set [ci].primary-version only when the primary version must not be the newest resolved version.

docs.text:

  • shared/setup/system-packages and shared/setup/build-command — test-job steps that run after this one and need vergil-tooling on PATH.
  • package/setup — checks the package toolchain image and installs only vergil-tooling in package build and install-test containers instead.

docs.title: CI Gate Requirements
docs.text: This section documents the CI gate configuration for all repositories consuming vergil-actions. It covers which checks are required and the security scanning requirements.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Every managed repository runs a common set of CI checks on pull requests. CI workflows trigger on pull_request only — push triggers are not used because branch protection enforces that all changes go through PRs.

Each check comes from a reusable workflow called by a job in the repository's ci.yml. GitHub names a reusable-workflow check <caller job> / <job>, so with the standard caller job keys the checks are grouped by workflow:

Caller job Workflow Purpose Example checks quality ci-quality.yml Common linting, custom validation, language lint and typecheck quality / evidence security ci-security.yml SAST and vulnerability scanning security / codeql, security / trivy, security / semgrep audit ci-audit.yml Dependency audit audit / evidence test ci-test.yml Unit tests test / evidence docs ci-docs.yml Strict docs build docs / docs version ci-version-bump.yml Version divergence gate version / version-bump package ci-package.yml .deb/.rpm build and install-test package / evidence

docs.title: Key concepts
docs.text:
• Reusable workflows — v2.0.0 introduced reusable CI workflows that produce the canonical check names automatically. Consuming repositories call these workflows rather than assembling jobs by hand.
  • Required status checks — Configured in GitHub repository rulesets. PRs cannot merge until all required checks pass.
  • Self-referencing CI — The vergil-actions repository tests its own actions using local paths (./actions/...).

docs.title: Pages in this section
docs.text:
• The All-Hard-Gates Principle — Why every check that matters is a hard, asserting gate and there are no report-only/warning gates
  • Required Checks — Which checks are required, and the check names each reusable workflow produces
  • Repository Rulesets — Branch protection, CI gates, and tag protection ruleset configuration
  • Security Scanning — CodeQL, Semgrep, and Trivy configuration details

docs.title: The All-Hard-Gates Principle
docs.text:
Every check that matters is a hard, asserting gate. There are no report-only or warning gates.

This is a foundational principle of the vergil CI model, not a style preference. It governs how every gate in the CI gate requirements is designed: a check either fails the build when it fires, or it does not exist.

docs.title: The principle
docs.text:
A gate has exactly two possible dispositions:

  • Pass — the condition it asserts holds; the build proceeds.
  • Fail — the condition does not hold; the build stops, loudly and terminally, until the underlying problem is fixed.

There is deliberately no third disposition. No check emits a warning that the build carries forward. No check writes an advisory that a human is trusted to notice later. If a condition is worth checking at all, it is worth failing on — so it is a hard gate.

docs.title: Why warnings are worthless here
docs.text:
A warning only has value if a human reliably acts on it. That assumption does not survive contact with how code actually gets merged.

At modern code-generation rates, the volume of change moving through review is far larger than the human attention available to scrutinize it. Reviewers optimize for the single question that governs the merge button: "Can I merge?" A warning does not block the merge, so it does not answer that question, so it does not get read. Once a change is merged, nobody revisits it to chase down a warning that was already, by definition, deemed non-blocking.

The operative failure mode

An unheeded warning is indistinguishable from no warning at all. A signal that no one is required to act on, and that no mechanism forces anyone to act on, is not a safeguard — it is noise that provides the appearance of a safeguard while delivering none of its protection.

So a report-only gate is worse than useless: it costs the same to build and run as a real gate, it clutters output, and it lulls the team into believing a class of problem is "covered" when in practice nothing stops that problem from shipping. The honest options are to assert it and fail on it, or to not check it at all. There is no coherent middle.

docs.title: Deprecation warnings are errors
docs.text:
Deprecation warnings are the clearest case, because they are not really warnings — they are early signal of a future outage. A deprecated API, flag, or action is announcing a date on which it will stop working. Left as a warning, that signal decays into background noise and is rediscovered only when the deprecation becomes a removal and the pipeline breaks in production.

Treating deprecation warnings as errors converts a future, unscheduled outage into a present, scheduled unit of work — surfaced while the context is fresh and the fix is cheap, instead of during the incident it would otherwise become. See [/vergil:deprecation-triage] for the workflow that turns each such error into a tracked decision.

docs.title: No five-page exception list
docs.text:
The failure mode this principle guards against is the sprawling warning-exception list: a document that accumulates "known" warnings, each with a rationale for why this one is tolerated, until the list is five pages long and no one can tell which entries still matter. Such a list is a graveyard of decisions no one is accountable for, and every entry is a place where a real regression can hide in plain sight.

The rule that prevents it is simple:

If it matters, assert it and fail on it. If it does not matter enough to fail on, do not check it.

This keeps the gate set small, meaningful, and trustworthy: every gate that exists is one the build genuinely depends on, and a green build is a categorical statement, not a statement with a footnote.

docs.title: The gate deployment lifecycle
docs.text:
Everything above describes gates in their steady state. There is one — and only one — situation in which a gate legitimately runs without failing the build: while it is being deployed. This does not contradict the all-hard-gates principle; it is how a hard gate is safely introduced.

Distinguish two things that a warning-emitting check might be:

  • A permanent soft gate — a check configured to warn and never fail, as its end state. This is the anti-pattern the rest of this document rejects. It does not exist in this model. There is no supported permanent configuration in which a check that matters merely warns.
  • A hard gate in warning mode — a temporary deployment state of a gate whose end state is enforcing. It is on a clock, it is owned, and it is committed to promotion.

Introducing a new hard gate is a lifecycle, not a flip of a switch:

  1. Warning mode (bake-in). The new gate runs on every build and reports its result, but does not fail the build, for a bounded bake-in period. During this window the team collects reliability data — false-positive rate, flakiness, performance, edge cases — and works the defects out. The gate is proving it is trustworthy enough to hold the merge button.
  2. Promotion. Once the gate is proven stable in production, it is promoted to enforcing mode: fatal, exactly like every other gate. The promotion is a deliberate, single act — ideally one flag flip — not a gradual erosion.

The distinction stated precisely

Warning mode is a hard gate in warning mode, never a soft gate. The difference is not the runtime behavior in the moment — both merely report — but the commitment: a hard gate in warning mode is time-boxed and owned, with enforcing as its scheduled, non-optional end state. The end state of every gate is enforcing. A warning with no promotion date and no owner is not a gate being deployed; it is the unheeded- warning anti-pattern wearing a lifecycle costume.

This refines, rather than softens, the earlier sections. "An unheeded warning is meaningless" is true of a permanent report-only gate precisely because nothing ever forces anyone to act on it. A hard gate in warning mode is the opposite: its promotion to fatal is the mechanism that forces the action, and the bake-in period exists only to earn the right to pull that trigger safely.

docs.title: Example: the CI-evidence gate
docs.text:
The CI-evidence completeness gate (epic vergil-project/.github#140) is the worked example of this lifecycle run to completion. It was introduced in warning mode: every release ran the evidence harvest and completeness check and reported the result, but a shortfall did not yet block the release. It baked across the normal release cadence — roughly four weeks — while its robustness (retry/backoff, idempotency, harvest completeness) was validated against real releases. Once it had proven stable, a single flag flip (evidence-enforce false→true) promoted it to enforcing.

That promotion is now live. The gate is enforcing in its steady state: an incomplete or failed evidence bundle is a terminal, publish-blocking failure, exactly like every other hard gate. It was never a permanent soft gate — warning mode was only the on-ramp, and the lifecycle has reached its enforcing end state.

Enforcement does not rely on the gate step's own failure propagating. In cd-release, the pre-publish CI evidence gate step and the post-release Attach CI evidence bundle step are each followed by an explicit enforcement guard step. In enforcing mode the guard fails the job when the evidence step's outcome is failure, or when the step reports success without the composite's positive output (passed=true for the gate, attached=true for the attach). The guard on the gate runs before anything is downloaded, built, tagged, or released. The guard on the attach runs after the Release exists, so its error states plainly that the release has already been published without its evidence bundle. Both guards were added after a release in which an enforcing gate failure was masked into a green step and the release published anyway (vergil-project/vergil-actions#925).

docs.title: Why this makes public evidence bundles safe
docs.text:
This principle is load-bearing for the CI-evidence archival work (epic vergil-project/.github#140). That epic publishes a complete, attested evidence bundle as a public asset on every release, capturing the output of every gate.

Bundling everything onto a public artifact is safe precisely because every gate is a hard gate. Evidence generation runs only after all gates are green, and because there are no report-only or warning gates, a bundle by construction reflects a passing run with no unremediated findings to expose. The publish-safety property (epic #140 spec §9.1) depends directly on this model:

The dependency is explicit

Introducing any soft or report-only gate in the future would break this boundary. A passing release could then carry non-fatal findings into a public bundle, and the publish-safety guarantee would have to be revisited. The all-hard-gates principle is therefore not just a code- quality stance — it is a precondition of safely publishing CI evidence.

Completeness is now measured against report payload, not merely artifact or envelope presence. A required gate that carries only an evidence.json envelope with no report payload fails the completeness check — envelope presence alone is no longer proof the gate ran (ref vergil-project/vergil-tooling#2812). The authoritative wire format for the bundle lives in vergil-tooling and is not duplicated here.

Every gate must therefore produce a real report file, including the quality gate of a language-less repo (container-suffix: base), whose lint and typecheck legs produce no reports. For those repos, the common job's transcript is the quality evidence. ci-quality captures the full output of vrg-validate --check common as quality-common.log (repo-profile, markdownlint, shellcheck, yamllint, hadolint, actionlint, ansible-lint), uploads it as the ci-evidence-quality-reports-common partial, and bundles it into ci-evidence-quality for every repo. As a result, the quality gate is never an evidence.json-only payload (vergil-project/vergil-actions#925). The custom job does the same for the repo's custom validator: it captures vrg-validate --check custom as quality-custom.log, uploads it as the ci-evidence-quality-reports-custom partial (tool vrg-validate-custom), and bundles it into ci-evidence-quality. A repo with no custom validator still ships the file, holding the one "no custom validator" line (vergil-project/.github#488).

Current residual

One known gap remains open, tracked as a limitation rather than done: the manifest metrics object is currently empty ({}). The security evidence.json tools array names the scanners whose SARIF the gate holds (vergil-project/vergil-actions#1215).

docs.text:

  • Security Scanning — the CodeQL, Semgrep, and Trivy gates, each a hard gate.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
All managed repositories use GitHub's repository rulesets (not legacy branch protection rules) to enforce merge requirements. Every repository has the same six rulesets, as vergil-tooling's desired state defines them (see its config audit reference). A docs-single-branch repository has no main branch, so it has five: it has no CI gates (main) ruleset.

Ruleset Target Purpose Branch protection main, develop PR requirements, deletion and force-push prevention CI gates (develop) develop Required status checks; the branch need not be up to date CI gates (main) main Required status checks; the branch must be up to date Tag protection v*.*.* and v*.* tags Protect release tags and rolling minor tags Rolling tag branch names refs/heads/v[0-9]* Block branches named like a rolling tag Automation branches refs/heads/automation/** Only the org automation App and the repository Admin role may create, update or force-push these branches

docs.title: Branch protection ruleset
docs.text:
Applies to both main and develop branches across all repositories.

Setting Value Require pull request Yes Required approving review count 0 Dismiss stale reviews on push Yes Require code owner review No Require last push approval No Require review thread resolution No Allowed merge methods merge, squash, rebase Block deletion Yes Block non-fast-forward Yes Bypass actors None (current_user_can_bypass: never)

Zero required approvals

The required approving review count is set to 0. PRs still require a pull request (direct pushes are blocked), but self-approval is permitted. This is appropriate for single-maintainer repositories.

docs.title: CI gates rulesets
docs.text: Two rulesets hold the required status checks that must pass before a PR can merge, one per branch. Both require the same checks. They differ only in whether a PR's branch must be up to date with its base before it merges.

docs.title: CI gates (develop)
docs.text:
Applies to develop (refs/heads/develop) in every repository, docs-single-branch repositories included.

Setting Value Strict required status checks No Do not enforce on create No

docs.title: CI gates (main)
docs.text:
Applies to main (refs/heads/main). A docs-single-branch repository has no main branch and no such ruleset.

Setting Value Strict required status checks Yes (branch must be up to date) Do not enforce on create No

docs.title: Why develop does not require up-to-date branches
docs.text:
Requiring a PR's branch to be up to date serializes merging: each merge into develop leaves every other open PR BEHIND, and each must update and run CI again. GitHub auto-merge never updates a BEHIND branch, so a batch of auto-merged PRs would wait forever. The check that the combined change works moves later; it does not disappear. A textual conflict surfaces at merge time. A semantic break between two individually green PRs is caught by the local vrg-validate that vrg-finalize-pr runs on the synced develop after the batch merges. And the develop → main release PR runs full CI against main, which keeps the up-to-date rule. A docs-single-branch repository has no release path, so for it the post-merge validate is the combined-change check. See epic 1218's spec, §2 for the full reasoning.

OpenSSF Scorecard

The Scorecard's Branch-Protection check lists "'up-to-date branches' is required to merge on branch 'develop'" among its items. With develop's ruleset no longer strict, later snapshots drop that item. This is accepted: it is a deliberate trade, for the reason above, not a hardening regression to fix.

docs.title: The required checks
docs.text: vrg-github-repo-config derives the required checks from each repository's vergil.toml, so the set depends on the repository's configuration. Both CI gates rulesets carry the same set. See the required check set for the full list and the condition under which each check is required.

docs.title: Example: a public Python library
docs.text:
A public Python library that publishes docs and has a release model gets:

quality / evidence
security / trivy
security / semgrep
docs / docs
Trivy
Semgrep OSS
security / codeql
CodeQL
audit / evidence
test / evidence
version / version-bump

Trivy, Semgrep OSS and CodeQL are GitHub code scanning checks, required because GHAS is available on a public repository. A repository with a [package] section also requires package / evidence.

Version-agnostic evidence gates

The matrixed workflows (ci-audit, ci-quality, ci-test) take their version matrix from vrg-ci-resolve, which resolves vergil.toml against the published language version window, so the per-version legs (unit / 3.14, lint / 3.13, …) change whenever the resolved set changes: the window gains or drops a version, or the [ci].versions pin changes. Branch protection therefore requires the stable <kind> / evidence aggregate gates — audit / evidence, quality / evidence, test / evidence — not the per-version legs. Each evidence job runs with if: always() and asserts every leg succeeded, so a failed or skipped leg fails the aggregate red. A change to the resolved set changes the legs but not the required-check set. See Evidence gates are the required checks.

docs.title: Example: vergil-actions
docs.text:
This repository declares no primary language in vergil.toml (its ci.yml passes language: shell to the workflows), so it gets no CodeQL checks and no audit or test evidence gates. It requires only the always-required checks (including quality / evidence), the docs gate, the Trivy and Semgrep code scanning checks, and the version gate:

quality / evidence
security / trivy
security / semgrep
docs / docs
Trivy
Semgrep OSS
version / version-bump

Shell linting (shellcheck, actionlint and the other common linters) runs inside quality / common, which is not required on its own: it gates the merge through quality / evidence, as does quality / custom.

docs.title: Tag protection ruleset
docs.text:
Applies to the full semver release tags (such as v1.1.1 or v2.0.0) and to the rolling minor tags (such as v1.1) that consumers follow as their deploy ref. Only the repository Admin role and the org automation App may create, move or delete either: the release workflow pushes each vX.Y.Z tag with the App's installation token.

Setting Value Patterns refs/tags/v*.*.*, refs/tags/v*.* Restrict creations Yes Block deletion Yes Block non-fast-forward Yes Block update Yes Bypass actors The org automation App (Integration, its per-org App ID, bypass_mode: always) and the repository Admin role (RepositoryRole, actor_id: 5, bypass_mode: always)

docs.title: Why both v*.*.* and v*.*
docs.text: A rolling minor tag (e.g., v1.1) always points to the latest patch release, and consumers reference it to receive patch updates automatically. A consumer that follows v1.1 runs whatever the tag points to, so moving it is as sensitive as moving a release tag. v*.*.* covers the immutable release tags (v1.1.1, v1.1.2); v*.* covers the rolling tags. The publish workflow's tag-and-release action no longer moves rolling tags: vrg-promote moves them in the release orchestrator's promote phase (see cd/release/tag-and-release).

docs.title: Bypass actors
docs.text: The ruleset has two bypass actors. The org automation App creates the vX.Y.Z release tags: the cd/release/tag-and-release action pushes them with the App's installation token, never the workflow's GITHUB_TOKEN (see CD release). The repository Admin role is the human release identity, so moving a rolling tag to a new patch release with vrg-promote and cleanup operations (e.g., removing a tag created against the wrong branch) both run under it. No other identity, the agent Apps and the GitHub Actions integration included, can create, move or delete a protected tag: a bypass for the GitHub Actions integration would let any workflow's GITHUB_TOKEN create a release tag. The App's numeric ID differs per org, as for the Automation branches ruleset.

docs.title: Rolling tag branch names ruleset
docs.text:
Blocks any branch whose name has the shape of a rolling tag. Some consumers, Claude Code among them, resolve a ref such as v2.1 as a branch before a tag (git's own short-name lookup prefers the tag), so for them the rolling tag's protection holds only while no branch of that name can exist.

Setting Value Pattern refs/heads/v[0-9]* Restrict creation Yes Restrict update Yes Block non-fast-forward Yes Bypass actors None

The pattern is a v followed by a digit, so names such as vm-… stay available. Deletion is not restricted, so a stray branch of that shape can still be removed.

docs.title: Automation branches ruleset
docs.text:
Mechanized jobs, such as the nightly github-config job, push to automation/<job>/<run-id> branches and open a PR that merges through GitHub auto-merge with no human in the loop. Without this ruleset any identity with Contents write, every agent App included, could push to such a branch and have its content merged into develop.

Setting Value Pattern refs/heads/automation/** Restrict creation Yes Restrict update Yes Block non-fast-forward Yes Bypass actors The org automation App (Integration, its per-org App ID, bypass_mode: always) and the repository Admin role (RepositoryRole, actor_id: 5, bypass_mode: always)

Deletion is not restricted: automation branches are temporary, removed by delete-on-merge and by each run of their job. The App's numeric ID differs per org; vrg-github-repo-config looks it up from the App's slug in the VRG_AUTOMATION_APP Actions variable.

docs.title: Adding a new required check
docs.text:
When adding a new CI job that should block merges:

  1. Add the job to the CI workflow.
  2. Open a PR and verify the check runs and passes.
  3. Do not add the check by hand under Settings > Rules. vrg-github-repo-config derives the required-check set itself (from desired_ci_gates_rulesets() in vergil-tooling and the repository's vergil.toml), and the nightly ops-github-config run of vrg-github-repo-config update converges both CI gates rulesets back to that set, removing a hand-added check. Add the check to that derivation in vergil-tooling; once that change is released, the next nightly run (or vrg-github-repo-config update run by hand) converges the rulesets.
  4. Verify the check name matches exactly. For the matrixed workflows, require the stable <kind> / evidence aggregate (e.g. test / evidence), not the per-version legs — the legs change with the resolved version set (the window or the [ci].versions pin), the aggregate does not.

docs.title: Branch targeting
docs.text:
The rulesets that protect main and develop use explicit branch references (refs/heads/main, refs/heads/develop). Never use ~DEFAULT_BRANCH in ruleset conditions.

The ~DEFAULT_BRANCH macro resolves to the repository's configured default branch. In this project family, the default branch is develop (not main), so ~DEFAULT_BRANCH resolves to develop — silently leaving main unprotected. Always use explicit refs/heads/ references for both branches.

docs.title: Modifying rulesets via API
docs.text:
Do not edit rulesets with raw gh api calls. vrg-github-repo-config computes the desired rulesets from the repository's vergil.toml and converges GitHub to them through the API:

# Report drift in the local files and the GitHub configuration.
# Exit 0 = compliant, 1 = drift, 2 = the audit could not complete.
vrg-github-repo-config audit --repo vergil-project/{repo}

# Report the GitHub configuration differences only. Exit 0 whether or not
# there is drift; 2 = it could not complete or a setting is not checked.
vrg-github-repo-config diff --repo vergil-project/{repo}

# Reconcile the GitHub configuration, including the rulesets, and open one
# sync PR for any drifted managed file
vrg-github-repo-config update --repo vergil-project/{repo}

--repo defaults to the current directory's git remote. The local file checks run against a fresh clone of the repository's develop, never the current directory. vergil.toml is read from the develop branch; --config PATH uses a local copy instead. apply, which reconciles only the GitHub configuration, is deprecated in favour of update.

To change a ruleset, change the vergil.toml that it is derived from and merge the change to develop; the nightly ops-github-config run of update converges the ruleset, or run update by hand. A ruleset edited by hand is converged back by that nightly run. See the vergil-tooling GitHub config audit reference for the full list of checks.

docs.title: Required check set
docs.text:
The required status checks live in the two CI gates rulesets, CI gates (develop) and CI gates (main), which require the same set. vrg-github-repo-config in vergil-tooling derives them from each repository's vergil.toml, so the set depends on the repository's configuration rather than a fixed category. Check names assume the standard caller job keys (quality, security, docs, audit, test, package, version), because GitHub names a reusable-workflow check <caller job> / <job>.

Required check Produced by Required when quality / evidence ci-quality.yml Always security / trivy ci-security.yml Always security / semgrep ci-security.yml Always docs / docs ci-docs.yml The repo publishes docs ([publish].docs) Trivy, Semgrep OSS GitHub code scanning (SARIF upload) Always security / codeql, CodeQL ci-security.yml, GitHub code scanning The primary language is supported by CodeQL audit / evidence ci-audit.yml The language has a dependency-audit check test / evidence ci-test.yml The language has a unit-test check package / evidence ci-package.yml vergil.toml has a [package] section version / version-bump ci-version-bump.yml The repo has a release model (not none)

Trivy, Semgrep OSS and CodeQL are the SARIF analysis checks that GitHub creates when scanner results are uploaded to code scanning; see Security Scanning. Every repository is public, so GHAS is always available and these checks always report.

docs.title: Evidence gates are the required checks
docs.text:
The matrixed reusable workflows (ci-audit, ci-quality, ci-test) take their version matrix from vrg-ci-resolve at run time, which resolves the consumer's vergil.toml against the published language version window (see Reusable Workflows). Because the number and names of the per-version legs change whenever the resolved set changes (the window gains or drops a version, or the [ci].versions pin changes), the per-version legs are not the required checks. Requiring them would force a ruleset edit every time a version was added or dropped.

Instead, each matrixed workflow emits one stable, version-agnostic aggregate gate named <kind> / evidence:

Workflow Required aggregate gate ci-audit.yml audit / evidence ci-quality.yml quality / evidence ci-test.yml test / evidence ci-package.yml package / evidence (repos with [package] only)

A repo whose vergil.toml has a [package] section calls ci-package.yml under a caller job keyed package, and package / evidence is a required check for it. Its build and install-test legs vary with the [package] targets and the matrix tier, so, as with the version legs, only the aggregate gate is required. Repos without [package] do not call ci-package.yml and do not require the gate.

The evidence job needs every matrix leg for its kind and runs with if: always(), then asserts each leg's result is success before emitting. A failed or skipped leg therefore makes the aggregate gate fail red rather than skip green — closing the "green by absence" hole where a skipped leg would otherwise leave the gate unset and non-blocking. Branch protection requires these stable gates (plus package / evidence for [package] repos); the per-version legs run and appear in the checks UI but are informational, so the required-check set does not churn when the resolved version set changes.

quality / evidence also aggregates the non-matrixed quality / common and quality / custom jobs: it needs common, custom, lint and typecheck and fails if any of them did not succeed. That holds in every repo, whatever its language, so quality / evidence is required everywhere. quality / common and quality / custom still run but are not required on their own; a failing common linter or custom validator blocks the merge through quality / evidence, even in a repo with no primary language.

ci-security.yml also has an evidence job (security / evidence), but it is not a required check: the scanner jobs are not matrixed, so they are required directly.

docs.title: Reusable workflow check-name mapping
docs.text:
Each reusable workflow produces the check names below, shown with the standard caller job key as the prefix. See Reusable Workflows for full details. For the matrixed workflows the required check is the version-agnostic <kind> / evidence aggregate; the per-version legs are informational (see Evidence gates are the required checks above).

Workflow Check names produced Required check ci-docs.yml docs / docs docs / docs (repos that publish docs) ci-security.yml security / codeql, security / trivy, security / semgrep, security / evidence security / trivy, security / semgrep; security / codeql with a CodeQL-supported language ci-quality.yml quality / matrix, quality / setup, quality / common, quality / custom, quality / lint / <version>, quality / typecheck / <version> legs + quality / evidence aggregate quality / evidence ci-audit.yml audit / matrix, audit / dependencies / <version> legs + audit / evidence aggregate audit / evidence ci-test.yml test / matrix, test / unit / <version> legs + test / evidence aggregate test / evidence ci-version-bump.yml version / setup, version / version-bump version / version-bump (repos with a release model) ci-package.yml ([package] repos only) package / matrix, package / build / <cell>, package / install-test / <cell> legs + package / evidence aggregate package / evidence

docs.title: ci-security.yml flags
docs.text:
The ci-security.yml reusable workflow accepts these flags to control which scanner jobs run (see ci-security for every input):

Flag Controls Default run-security security / codeql, security / trivy, security / semgrep jobs true run-codeql security / codeql job (requires run-security to also be true) true 
security:
  uses: vergil-project/vergil-actions/.github/workflows/ci-security.yml@v2.1
  permissions:
    contents: read
    security-events: write
  with:
    language: <lang>

docs.title: Ruleset configuration
docs.text: All required status checks are enforced via GitHub repository rulesets, not legacy branch protection rules. Each branch has its own CI gates ruleset with the same required checks: CI gates (develop) does not require a PR's branch to be up to date, and CI gates (main) does (why). See Repository Rulesets for full configuration details including branch protection, CI gates, and tag protection.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Three security scanning tools provide layered coverage:

Tool Purpose Output CodeQL GitHub-native SAST with deep semantic analysis SARIF uploaded to code scanning Semgrep Fast pattern-based SAST with community rulesets SARIF uploaded to code scanning Trivy Dependency vulnerability scanning and SBOM generation SARIF uploaded to code scanning

docs.title: GHAS requirements
docs.text: All three tools upload results in SARIF format to GitHub Code Scanning, which requires GitHub Advanced Security (GHAS). GHAS is available by default, at no cost, on public repositories. Every repository is public, so GHAS is always available.

docs.title: Accepted suppressions: uploaded SARIF vs. evidence
docs.text:
The SARIF gate passes a finding that has been accepted in source (for example a justified # nosemgrep: …), but GitHub code scanning does not honor SARIF suppressions and would still fail the scanner's SARIF analysis check (e.g. Semgrep OSS) on it. To keep the two in agreement, the Semgrep and Trivy actions run vrg-sarif-filter before uploading and send code scanning a filtered copy (*.upload.sarif) with accepted-suppressed results removed, using the same semantics as the gate.

The unfiltered SARIF (semgrep-results.sarif, trivy-results.sarif) is what the security / evidence job collects into the ci-evidence-security bundle, so every accepted suppression remains auditable there.

CodeQL is not filtered: github/codeql-action/analyze uploads its results itself, so there is no separate upload step to hand a filtered file to.

docs.title: Check names in the PR status area
docs.text:
Each security scanner uploads its SARIF to code scanning, so it produces two check runs on a pull request:

CI workflow job SARIF analysis check security / codeql CodeQL security / semgrep Semgrep OSS security / trivy Trivy

The first column shows the ci-security jobs, named <caller job> / <job> with the standard security caller job key. The second column shows the checks GitHub code scanning creates when the SARIF results are uploaded (this needs the security-events: write permission).

Both columns are gated in both CI gates rulesets, CI gates (develop) and CI gates (main):

  • security / trivy and security / semgrep are always required.
  • Trivy and Semgrep OSS are always required.
  • security / codeql and CodeQL are required when the repository's primary language is supported by CodeQL.

See Required Checks for the full required set.

docs.title: Viewing results
docs.text:
Security scan results appear in the repository's Security tab:

  1. Navigate to Security > Code scanning alerts.
  2. Filter by tool: CodeQL, semgrep, or trivy-fs / trivy-image.
  3. Each alert shows the affected file, line number, severity, and a description of the finding.

docs.title: CodeQL
docs.text:
CodeQL performs deep semantic analysis of source code. It understands data flow, control flow, and language-specific patterns.

  • Languages scanned: Python, Go, Rust, C++ and TypeScript.
  • Query suite: +security-extended (default) includes the standard security queries plus extended checks.
  • Autobuild: CodeQL automatically detects the build system and compiles the project.
- uses: vergil-project/vergil-actions/actions/ci/security/codeql@v2.1
  with:
    language: python

docs.title: Semgrep
docs.text:
Semgrep provides fast, pattern-based static analysis with a large library of community-maintained rules.

Default rulesets enabled for every scan:

  • p/<language> — Language-specific security rules
  • p/security-audit — Cross-cutting security audit rules
  • p/secrets — Secret detection (API keys, tokens, passwords)

Additional rulesets can be added via extra-config:

- uses: vergil-project/vergil-actions/actions/ci/security/semgrep@v2.1
  with:
    language: golang
    extra-config: "p/owasp-top-ten"

docs.title: Trivy
docs.text: Trivy scans for known vulnerabilities in dependencies and container images.

docs.title: Scan modes
docs.text: Mode Use case SARIF category fs Scan project dependencies for known CVEs trivy-fs image Scan container images for OS and library CVEs trivy-image sbom Generate CycloneDX SBOM (no SARIF upload) —

docs.title: Severity filtering
docs.text:
By default, only CRITICAL and HIGH severity vulnerabilities are reported. This can be adjusted:

- uses: vergil-project/vergil-actions/actions/shared/security/trivy@v2.1
  with:
    scan-type: fs
    severity: "CRITICAL,HIGH,MEDIUM"

docs.title: Exit code behavior
docs.text:
By default, Trivy exits with code 1 when vulnerabilities are found, failing the CI check. Set exit-code: "0" for advisory-only mode:

- uses: vergil-project/vergil-actions/actions/shared/security/trivy@v2.1
  with:
    scan-type: fs
    exit-code: "0"

docs.title: Workflow permissions
docs.text:
All security scanning jobs require the security-events: write permission:

jobs:
  codeql:
    permissions:
      security-events: write
      contents: read

docs.title: Development
docs.text: This section covers development workflow, environment setup, validation, and contribution guidelines for the vergil-actions repository.

docs.title: Pages in this section
docs.text:
• Environment and Tooling — External tool dependencies and git hooks setup
  • Validation — Local validation commands and the dispatch architecture
  • Contributing — How to add or modify actions, testing via self-referencing CI, and the commit/PR workflow

docs.title: Adding a new action
docs.text:
1. Create a directory under actions/ following the namespace convention: actions/{phase}/{domain}/{action}/action.yml. The phase is one of:

    Phase Use for Example ci Pre-merge checks, consumed by the ci-* workflows ci/security/codeql cd Post-merge release and deploy, consumed by the cd-* workflows cd/release/tag-and-release ops Scheduled repository maintenance, consumed by the ops-* workflows ops/github-config/branch-sweep package .deb/.rpm package builds, consumed by ci-package and cd-release package/setup shared Actions used by more than one phase shared/setup/vergil local Actions used only by this repository's own workflows local/freeze-internal-refs

    For ci, cd and ops the domain matches the workflow that consumes the action (ci/security/* for ci-security.yml, ops/github-config/* for ops-github-config.yml). An action used by several workflows in one phase takes a descriptive domain instead (ci/evidence/emit).

    Two actions sit directly under their phase, with no domain: package/setup, the only action in the package phase, and ci/matrix. New actions use the three-level layout. 2. Define the action as a composite action — no custom JavaScript or Docker actions. 3. Include clear name, description, inputs, and outputs in action.yml. 4. Put supporting scripts next to action.yml in the action directory (e.g. actions/shared/setup/vergil/derive.sh) and call them through ${GITHUB_ACTION_PATH}. Put their tests in a tests/ subdirectory, as <name>.test.sh scripts committed executable (git mode 100755: run chmod +x before git add). Validation fails on any *.test.sh with another mode; see Validation. 5. Add the action to the appropriate workflow using a local path reference (./actions/{phase}/{domain}/{action}). 6. Add a documentation page under docs/site/docs/actions/ and update the nav in docs/site/mkdocs.yml. 7. Run each test script from a workflow, as bash <path> in a step (most action harnesses run in smoke-setup-vergil.yml). Validation fails on any *.test.sh that no workflow and no part of validation runs; see Validation. A new smoke-*.yml workflow also needs a workflow_call trigger and a job in nightly-harnesses.yml; see Nightly harness run.

docs.title: Composite action design rules
docs.text:
• Shell steps only — Use shell: bash for all run steps.
  • No secrets access — Composite actions cannot access secrets directly. Callers must pass secrets as inputs.
  • Idempotent when possible — Actions should be safe to re-run (e.g., cd/release/tag-and-release skips if the tag exists).
  • Environment variables for sensitive data — Use env blocks rather than inline interpolation for values that might contain special characters.

docs.title: Reusable workflow caller contract
docs.text:
The permissions: blocks of a workflow_call workflow — workflow-level and job-level alike — are requests against the caller, not grants. GitHub validates at workflow startup that the calling job's effective permissions cover every requested scope; a caller that does not is rejected with startup_failure before any job runs, and no checks are registered on the PR.

Treat any addition to a permissions: block in a workflow_call workflow as a breaking change to the caller contract:

  • It requires a coordinated consumer rollout: every consumer must add the grant to its calling job before the rolling tag is promoted to a release containing the new request. Grants are backward-compatible (callers may grant more than a called workflow requests), so consumer patches can always land first.
  • Call the new requirement out prominently in the release notes, under a Breaking change heading.
  • Removing or narrowing a request is non-breaking and needs no rollout.

Incident #698 is the cautionary tale: v2.1.3 added actions: read to ci-security.yml's request and broke every consumer of @v2.1 at the moment of promote. Follow-ups #699 (consumer-refresh release stage) and #700 (release-gate permissions diff) track automating this policy.

docs.title: Testing via self-referencing CI
docs.text:
This repository tests its own actions by using local path references in its CI workflow (uses: ./.github/workflows/ci-quality.yml) and in the reusable workflows that call the composite actions:

- uses: ./actions/shared/setup/vergil   # Not the remote reference

When you modify an action, the PR's CI run uses your modified version. This provides integration testing without a separate test repository.

docs.title: Branching workflow
docs.text:
• Protected branches: main and develop — no direct commits.
  • Branch naming: work branches are <type>/<N>-<slug>, where <type> is feature, bugfix, hotfix or chore and <N> is the GitHub issue number (e.g. feature/42-add-check). release/* branches are created by vrg-release.
  • Feature and bugfix PRs target develop with squash merge.
  • Release PRs target main with regular merge.

docs.title: Committing
docs.text:
Always use vrg-commit:

vrg-commit \
  --type feat \
  --scope ci \
  --message "add new validation check"

Required flags:

  • --type: feat|fix|docs|style|refactor|test|chore|ci|build|revert
  • --scope: Conventional commit scope
  • --message: Commit description

Optional flags:

  • --body: Detailed commit body
  • --allow-empty: Allow a commit with no staged changes (e.g. to re-trigger CI)

docs.title: Submitting PRs
docs.text:
PR submission is split between the agent and the human. Agents never run vrg-submit-pr.

  1. Agent: push the branch, then record the PR metadata. Push the branch to origin first — report-ready pushes only its metadata ref, not the branch:

    vrg-git push -u origin feature/42-add-check
vrg-pr-workflow report-ready \
  --issue 42 \
  --title "feat(ci): add new validation check" \
  --summary "Add new validation check" \
  --notes "Validated with vrg-validate."

    --issue, --title, --summary and --notes are required and must be non-empty. --linkage defaults to Ref; leave it there, because vrg-submit-pr picks the keyword at submit time. If the change touches .github/workflows/**, GitHub refuses the agent's push; the human's vrg-submit-pr pushes the branch instead.

    report-ready freezes the branch: further commits and pushes are refused. Re-running it to correct the title, summary or notes is allowed. More work belongs in a new follow-up issue; vrg-pr-workflow unfreeze reopens a branch that has not been submitted.

  2. Human: submit the PR. Run vrg-submit-pr with no arguments from the worktree, or vrg-submit-pr <branch> [<branch> …] from the main worktree. It reads the recorded metadata, previews the PR and opens it after confirmation.

  3. Human: merge and clean up. Run vrg-finalize-pr, which waits for checks, merges the PR and removes the merged branch and worktree.

The recorded title, summary and notes are readable by anyone on a public repository, so they must not contain secrets.

docs.title: Git hooks
docs.text: No git hooks are installed and there is nothing to configure. Branch and commit rules, including the refusal to commit directly to the protected branches (develop, release, main), are enforced by the vergil-tooling vrg-git and vrg-commit wrappers and by PR CI. See the vergil-tooling validation matrix.

docs.title: Host prerequisites
docs.text:
Install the vergil-tooling host tool, which provides vrg-container-run, vrg-commit, vrg-validate, and other workflow commands, as vergil-tooling's Getting Started says. Its lines install one exact release tag, with its dependencies pinned by that tag's own uv.lock, on uv's managed Python.

Docker must be running for vrg-container-run to work.

docs.title: Validation and development tools
docs.text:
All validation tools (actionlint, shellcheck, markdownlint, yamllint) and documentation tools (mkdocs-material, mike) are pre-installed in the ghcr.io/vergil-project/prod-base:latest container image, the one vrg-container-run uses for a repo with no primary language, as here. vergil-tooling itself is not — on first use, vrg-container-run builds a per-branch cached image with vergil-tooling installed at the version pinned in vergil.toml, and rebuilds it when vergil.toml or the lockfiles change. No manual host installs are needed.

vrg-container-run -- vrg-validate     # Run all validation checks
vrg-container-docs serve              # Preview docs locally on port 8000
vrg-container-docs build --strict     # Strict docs build

Use vrg-container-docs for the docs: vrg-container-run publishes no port, so a mkdocs serve run through it is not reachable from a host browser.

docs.title: Canonical command
docs.text:
vrg-container-run -- vrg-validate

This runs all validation inside a per-branch cached container image that vrg-container-run builds on first use from ghcr.io/vergil-project/prod-base:latest: vergil-tooling is installed into it at the version pinned in vergil.toml ([dependencies] vergil), and the cache is rebuilt automatically when vergil.toml or the lockfiles change. No manual host installs are needed beyond the vergil-tooling host tool.

docs.title: Documentation build
docs.text:
Build and preview the docs site with vrg-container-docs, which runs mkdocs in the same prod-base image:

vrg-container-docs build --strict     # Strict docs build
vrg-container-docs serve              # Preview docs locally on port 8000

vrg-container-run publishes no port, so a mkdocs serve run through it is not reachable from a host browser.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text: vrg-validate reads primary_language from vergil.toml and runs common checks followed by language-specific checks from the built-in command registry. Common checks include repo-profile validation, markdownlint, shellcheck, yamllint, and actionlint.

docs.title: Custom checks
docs.text: After the common checks, vrg-validate runs the repository's own validator, scripts/bin/validate-custom (in CI, the quality / custom job). It runs the checks below, then the action test suites, then the checks' own tests in scripts/tests/.

docs.title: Test script modes
docs.text: The first check fails naming each *.test.sh tracked in git whose mode is not 100755 (executable). It checks the mode git records, not the one on disk, so fix an offender with chmod +x <path> and then git add <path>. An in-place edit (sed -i, perl -i) can replace a file and drop its executable bit, so check the mode after one with git ls-files -s <path>.

docs.title: Test suite wiring
docs.text: The second check, scripts/bin/check-test-suites-run, fails naming each *.test.sh tracked in git that nothing runs. A suite counts as run when a workflow under .github/workflows/ runs it by its repo-relative path (bash <path>, sh <path> or ./<path>) on a line that is not a comment, or when it sits directly in scripts/tests/, whose suites validate-custom runs. A path named only in a comment or outside a workflow does not count. The check reads the workflow text, so a step whose job never runs still counts.

docs.title: Early-exit pipes
docs.text: The third check, scripts/bin/check-early-exit-pipes, fails naming each line, in the *.sh, *.bash, *.yml and *.yaml files and scripts/bin/* tracked in git, where a pipeline feeds a consumer that exits before reading all its input: grep -q, grep -m, grep --quiet, --silent, --max-count or head. Under set -o pipefail, which every suite here and GitHub's default bash shell set, such a consumer exits on its first match, the producer dies of SIGPIPE writing its next line, and the pipeline fails although it matched. Test the output with no pipe instead: grep -q <pattern> <<<"$(<producer>)".

docs.title: Secret environments
docs.text:
The fourth check, scripts/bin/check-secret-environments, fails naming each workflow job that reads a secret able to write or act without declaring the environment that holds it. The automation App's keys and the registry publishing tokens live in each repository's automation environment, whose deployment-branch policy admits only develop and main, so a run from any other branch sees them unset. The package-signing keys live in their own single-branch environments.

It reads every tracked workflow and, for each job that runs steps, collects each secrets.<NAME> read inside a ${{ }} expression, in any case and skipping quoted strings. A job that calls a reusable workflow with uses: runs no steps, so the called workflow's jobs are the ones checked. Each secret is checked against the tables at the top of the script:

Table Secrets Required environment AUTOMATION_SECRETS APP_CLIENT_ID, APP_PRIVATE_KEY, CARGO_REGISTRY_TOKEN automation SIGNING_SECRETS PACKAGE_SIGNING_KEY, PACKAGE_SIGNING_PASSPHRASE package-signing or index-signing UNSCOPED_SECRETS GITHUB_TOKEN, CONAN_AUDIT_PROVIDER_TOKEN_CONANCENTER none, each with its reason

Nothing passes unclassified. The check also fails on:

  • a secret that no table lists;
  • a dynamic read of the secrets context (secrets[...], toJSON(secrets));
  • a secret read in the workflow-level env, which every job sees;
  • a workflow that does not parse.

To fix a failure, declare the job's environment (environment: automation, or the signing environment). An environment named by an expression, such as ${{ inputs.environment }}, never counts as either, so a job that reads an automation or signing secret must name its environment literally. A job that reads no such secret may use one. A new secret goes into the table for the environment that holds it. An unscoped entry needs a reason that says why any job may read it.

The check also fails a reusable workflow that declares a secret required: true under on.workflow_call.secrets while one of its jobs names no environment literally: no environment:, one without a name, one named by an expression, or a job that calls another reusable workflow, which cannot declare one. GitHub checks a called workflow's required secrets for each of its jobs, and a secret that exists only in an environment is not provided to a job that declares none, even through secrets: inherit, so GitHub refuses the whole call before any job starts (vergil-project/vergil-actions#1428). To fix it, declare the secret required: false and, in each job that reads it, fail loudly before using it when it is empty, naming the secret, as cd-release.yml's Require the automation App secrets step does. Never fall back to GITHUB_TOKEN.

docs.title: Nightly harness wiring
docs.text: The fifth check, scripts/bin/check-nightly-harnesses, fails unless .github/workflows/nightly-harnesses.yml calls every smoke workflow. Each tracked smoke-<name>.yml must declare a workflow_call trigger, and the nightly workflow must have a job <name> whose uses: is ./.github/workflows/smoke-<name>.yml. A job there that calls anything else fails too, and so does a nightly workflow without its schedule and workflow_dispatch triggers. See Nightly harness run.

docs.title: Action test suites
docs.text: validate-custom then runs every *.test.sh tracked in git directly in an actions/**/tests/ directory, from the repo root as CI does, and fails naming each suite that fails. A suite listed in CI_ONLY_ACTION_SUITES, at the top of scripts/bin/validate-custom, is skipped and named with its reason. It stays CI-only because it reaches a live service or needs a tool the validation image lacks. Each entry must name a tracked suite, so a renamed or removed suite fails the run until its entry is updated. A new suite runs in validation by default. The workflow that runs it in CI is still needed for the wiring check above.

docs.title: Nightly harness run
docs.text:
On a pull request, each smoke-*.yml workflow runs only when its own paths change. Its harnesses, though, run against the released vergil-tooling that vergil.toml's [dependencies] vergil pin installs: the newest v2.1.Z tag. So a vergil-tooling release can break a harness with no change here, and nothing would show it until an unrelated pull request ran that workflow.

.github/workflows/nightly-harnesses.yml closes that gap. Once a day, and on a manual workflow_dispatch, it calls every smoke workflow on develop. Its report job then records the run in the org's operations queue under the stable name harness-nightly, through the ops/report action:

  • a failed or cancelled run opens the ops: vergil-actions / harness-nightly failing issue, or comments on it when it is already open;
  • the first green run after a failure adds a recovery comment;
  • nothing closes the issue: whoever works the queue closes it.

The issue links the run. The run's log shows the vergil-tooling version installed and the harness case that failed.

A new smoke workflow needs a workflow_call trigger and its own job in nightly-harnesses.yml, with that job added to the report job's needs and results. The nightly harness wiring check and actions/ops/report/tests/reporting-jobs.test.sh each fail until it has them.

docs.title: Tooling
docs.text:
The static validation tools are baked into the prod-base container image:

Tool Purpose actionlint GitHub Actions workflow linter shellcheck Shell script static analysis markdownlint Markdown formatting linter yamllint YAML formatting linter

vrg-validate itself is not baked in — it arrives via the dynamic vergil-tooling install described above. No host-level installs of any of these tools are required.

docs.title: Bug fixes
docs.text:
• bootstrap standards documentation Add AGENTS.md and repository standards overlay. Normalize docs formatting for markdownlint and make docs validation bash-compatible.

  • add autobuild step for compiled language support CodeQL requires a build step between init and analyze for compiled languages (Java, Go, C++). The autobuild action handles this automatically and is a no-op for interpreted languages.

  • sync shared tooling to v1.0.2 Update sync-tooling.sh from standard-tooling v1.0.2:

  • Fix --actions-compat flag leaking during self-update re-exec

  • Add canonical source comment to repo-profile.sh

  • sync lint scripts from standards-and-conventions (#28) Accept git-generated Revert commit messages in the CI commit message validator and support cross-repo owner/repo#123 issue linkage in the PR issue linkage validator.

Ref wphillipmoore/mq-rest-admin-common#62

  • pass release notes via env var to prevent shell injection (#44)
  • fix(publish): pass release notes via env var to prevent shell injection

Backticks in markdown code fences within release-notes were interpreted as bash command substitution when directly interpolated via ${{ }}. This caused go get commands in installation examples to be executed during the release step.

Pass release-notes through an environment variable ($RELEASE_NOTES) instead, which is not subject to shell interpretation.

  • replace mapfile with bash 3.2-compatible alternative (#49) macOS ships bash 3.2 which lacks mapfile. Replace with a simple variable capture and xargs pipe.

  • update add-to-project action to v1.0.2 (#69)

  • resolve event-payload race in version-bump-pr issue linkage (#73) The action previously created the PR with a simple body then edited it to add issue linkage. The CI standards-compliance check reads the PR body from the event payload, which is frozen at PR creation time, so the linkage was never seen. This fix adds a tracking-issue input with auto-discovery fallback and constructs the complete body before PR creation, eliminating the race condition.

docs.title: Bug fixes
docs.text:
• fix version-bump regex and correct VERSION to 1.1.2 (#136) The capture group in version-regex was preserving the major.minor. prefix, then {version} inserted the full next version, producing 1.1.1.1.2 instead of 1.1.2. Removed the capture group so the entire match is replaced with the next version.

  • create placeholder releases/index.md when no releases exist (#148) Pre-release repositories have releases/index.md in their mkdocs nav but no release note files yet. With strict mode enabled, mkdocs aborts on the missing file. Generate a placeholder index when no releases/*.md files are found.

  • install Trivy binary directly to avoid setup-trivy cache fallback failure (#152) The aquasecurity/trivy-action setup-trivy mechanism has a broken cache miss fallback that attempts to clone the trivy repo from source, which fails with 'couldn't find remote ref refs/heads/main'. This replaces setup-trivy with a direct binary download from GitHub releases and passes skip-setup-trivy: true to trivy-action, giving us full control over the Trivy version.

  • use setup-trivy with cache disabled instead of manual binary download (#153) The previous fix attempted a manual curl download with an incorrect version/URL. This uses the official setup-trivy action with cache disabled to avoid the broken cache miss fallback, then passes skip-setup-trivy to trivy-action.

  • replace aquasecurity GitHub actions with Docker-based Trivy execution (#154) The aquasecurity/trivy GitHub repo is empty (HTTP 409: 'Git Repository is empty'), causing both setup-trivy and trivy-action to fail when attempting to clone it. This replaces all aquasecurity GitHub actions with direct docker run commands using the aquasec/trivy Docker Hub image, which is still available and up to date (v0.69.1). A new trivy-image input allows pinning the version.

docs.title: Features
docs.text:
• drop auto-merge from version-bump-pr composite (bump 1.2.0) (#193) Step 2 of 3 for the poll-and-merge rework (plugin#57).

The composite used to end with:

gh pr merge --auto --merge --delete-branch <branch>

That call has been silently failing on every publish run since auto-merge was disabled fleet-wide — the bump PR got created, the step threw, the workflow was marked failure, and the user merged manually anyway.

Drop it. pr-url is already an output; the release skill drives the merge via st-merge-when-green once CI is green.

Action name / description, in-file comment, and public docs all updated to match. No other auto-merge references in the repo.

docs.title: Bug fixes
docs.text:
• use env vars + quoted heredoc in version-bump-pr Update step Surfaced on wphillipmoore/standard-tooling-plugin#78 (v1.4.1 publish): version-regex (\s*"version":\s*").*("\s*) contains literal double-quotes; GitHub expression interpolation put the raw value into the bash python3 -c "..." string, bash's outer double-quote closed at the first embedded ", the ( in the regex became a subshell-open, and the ) produced "unexpected token" at exit.

Latent since the step was written. Only surfaced once earlier composite failures (CHANGELOG merge, missing version-replacement) stopped masking it.

docs.title: Fix
docs.text:
Pass values via env: and use a single-quoted heredoc delimiter <<'PYEOF' so bash performs zero interpolation on the body. The regex, replacement, and next version are all read from os.environ inside the python block.

No caller-visible change to the composite's interface (same inputs, same behavior). Patch-level bump — v1.2.0 consumers automatically get the fix when v1.2 rolls forward.

docs.title: Bug fixes
docs.text: • map go to p/golang and capture scan exit codes The Semgrep registry uses p/golang, not p/go (HTTP 404). Added a language-name mapping so callers passing language: go get the correct ruleset. Also capture semgrep scan exit codes instead of letting bash -e kill the step, so the SARIF analysis step can provide diagnostics when the scan fails.

docs.title: Bug fixes
docs.text:
• handle missing primary-language in vergil.toml Use .get() with empty-string fallback instead of hard subscript when reading primary-language from vergil.toml. The key was removed in PR #609 but the docs deploy action still read it with a bare subscript, causing a KeyError in downstream CD pipelines. Ref #617

  • revert internal refs to @develop and replace trivy shell with vrg-trivy-scan All internal action references in reusable workflows were incorrectly frozen to @v2.0 on the develop branch. This broke self-referencing CI: changes merged to develop were never tested because workflows referenced old tagged code instead of the current branch. Reverted all 18 @v2.0 refs back to @develop so vrg-freeze-refs can properly rewrite them to exact patch versions at release time. Also replaced 80 lines of nested-shell-in-Docker trivy scan orchestration with vrg-trivy-scan, added Install vergil-tooling steps to codeql/trivy/semgrep jobs that were missing them. Ref #607, Ref #613

  • use local action paths for true self-referencing CI Replace all @develop action refs in reusable workflows with ./actions/ local paths. GitHub resolves ./ relative to the workflow file at the ref it was loaded from, so: during PR CI the actions come from the PR branch (true self-referencing), and at release time vrg-freeze-refs rewrites them to absolute tagged refs for downstream consumers. Ref #607, Ref #613

  • run trivy job in prod-base container Run the trivy CI job in the standard prod-base container instead of bare ubuntu-latest. This provides uv and other tooling needed by the Install vergil-tooling step. Ref #607

  • revert trivy action to original inline Docker approach Revert the trivy action to its original inline Docker implementation. The vrg-trivy-scan tool incorrectly wraps trivy in docker run rather than calling it directly, which needs to be fixed in vergil-tooling before the action can use it. See vergil-tooling#1246. Ref #607

  • use dev container prefix for CI Switch CI to use dev-base container images so we can test with updated container images before they are promoted to prod. Ref #607

  • eliminate shell injection patterns in action YAML files Move all expression interpolations out of run: script bodies and into env: blocks, referencing them as shell variables instead. This prevents expression injection where crafted input values could execute arbitrary commands during template expansion. Also fixes a bug in docs/deploy where the mike-command resolution step was referencing its own output instead of the input.

  • replace Docker orchestration with vrg-trivy-scan direct invocation Replace docker run wrapping in the trivy action with calls to vrg-trivy-scan for fs/image scans and direct trivy CLI for SBOM generation. The trivy job now runs in the container where trivy and vergil-tooling are available. Removes trivy-image and scanners inputs (no longer needed). Also converts the registry-publish trivy reference from @develop to local path.

docs.title: Refactoring
docs.text:
• replace inline shell with vrg-semgrep-scan Replace 70 lines of embedded shell (ruleset resolution, scan execution, jq-based SARIF evaluation) with a single call to vrg-semgrep-scan from vergil-tooling. The tool handles language-to-ruleset mapping, scan execution with structured exit codes, SARIF parsing, finding evaluation, and GitHub Actions job summaries. The action retains Dockerfile/workflow auto-detection as lightweight shell checks that set --has-dockerfiles and --has-workflows flags. Ref #597

  • replace inline SARIF evaluation with vrg-sarif-evaluate Replace 27 lines of jq-based SARIF evaluation shell (nullglob, slurp, filtering, gating) with a single call to vrg-sarif-evaluate from vergil-tooling. The tool handles directory-mode SARIF parsing, severity filtering, structured annotations, and job summaries. Ref #598

  • replace inlined Python scripts with vrg-docs-stage and vrg-docs-patch-nav Replace two inlined Python heredoc scripts (release notes staging with semver-sorted index generation, and mkdocs.yml nav patching) with calls to vrg-docs-stage and vrg-docs-patch-nav from vergil-tooling. Eliminates the container path workaround from issue #204. Ref #599

  • replace case-statement command derivation with vrg-ecosystem-resolve Replace three duplicated case blocks (build command, publish command, credential secret) with a single call to vrg-ecosystem-resolve from vergil-tooling. The tool writes shell-compatible strings directly to GITHUB_OUTPUT with the correct key names. User overrides append after the tool call (last write wins). Ref #600

  • replace inline validation with vrg-release-validate-inputs Replace interdependent conditionals, loop-based language validation, and duplicated supported-languages list with a single call to vrg-release-validate-inputs from vergil-tooling. The tool shares the canonical language list with vrg-ecosystem-resolve. Ref #601

  • replace inline sed/grep logic with vrg-freeze-refs Replace two shell steps (sed-based regex freezing with temp file cleanup, and duplicated find/grep validation) with a single vrg-freeze-refs call from vergil-tooling. The tool handles YAML file collection, reference freezing, and unfrozen-ref validation in one pass. Ref #602

  • remove redundant auto-close check already handled by vrg-pr-issue-linkage The vrg-pr-issue-linkage tool already validates both issue linkage and auto-close keyword rejection. The inline shell step duplicated the auto-close check with jq extraction and grep regex. Ref #604

  • replace inline comparison with vrg-version-divergence Replace 22 lines of version comparison shell (conditional extraction, string comparison, multi-path output writes) with a single call to vrg-version-divergence from vergil-tooling. The tool handles version comparison logic, error messages, and job summaries. The action retains version extraction via user-provided commands and maps the exit code to the diverged boolean output. Ref #605

  • replace sed TOML parsing with python3 tomllib Replace the fragile sed regex that extracts the vergil version from vergil.toml with a python3 one-liner using the stdlib tomllib module. The sed approach could not handle comments, multi-line values, or quoted strings correctly. The vrg-resolve-tooling-version tool exists in vergil-tooling but cannot be used here due to a bootstrapping constraint: this action is what installs vergil-tooling, so the tool is not yet available when the action runs. Ref #606

docs.title: Bug fixes
docs.text:
• install uv via setup-uv when not present on bare runners The vergil-tooling setup action assumed uv was pre-installed, which breaks on bare ubuntu-latest runners used by CD pipelines. Add a conditional astral-sh/setup-uv step that only runs when uv is not found on PATH.

Replace duplicated vergil-tooling install logic in the Trivy action with delegation to the setup action, establishing a single source of truth for the install path.

  • use astral-sh/setup-uv@v7 (v8 has no rolling major tag)
  • use pip to install uv on bare runners instead of astral-sh/setup-uv Replace astral-sh/setup-uv with pip install to avoid a circular dependency: the repo allowlist compliance check rejects astral-sh/* until vergil-tooling is updated, but vergil-tooling can't be fixed until this action works on bare runners.

The pip approach matches how the Docker base images install uv and has no external action dependency. A follow-up issue (#643) tracks upgrading to astral-sh/setup-uv once the allowlist and compliance tooling are updated.

docs.title: Bug fixes
docs.text:
• revert to Docker-based approach for bare-runner compatibility The vrg-trivy-scan rewrite (commits 3e3f333b through c4956a80) broke CD pipelines on bare ubuntu-latest runners where the trivy binary is not installed. Restore the Docker-based approach that brings its own Trivy via aquasec/trivy:0.70.0, with injection-safe env: blocks (from 7290af2d).

Also remove the container directive from the ci-security trivy job since Docker-based Trivy runs on the host and does not need a container image.

docs.title: Bug fixes
docs.text: • separate language and container-suffix inputs in cd-release.yml Add dedicated container-suffix input so non-language projects no longer misuse language: base. The container image line falls back through container-suffix, language, then 'base'. The validate-inputs action now treats language as optional and only passes it to the CLI when non-empty. Ref #653

docs.title: Bug fixes
docs.text:
• run codeql on bare runner so autobuild has a language toolchain Commit 4d942b5b moved the codeql job into the prod-base container to silence 'uv: command not found' (ref #636), but prod-base ships no language toolchain. CodeQL autobuild for compiled languages (go, java, rust) needs the compiler on PATH, so it failed fleet-wide with 'go: executable file not found in $PATH' on every consuming repo pinned to @v2.0.

Language images are published per-version only (prod-go:1.25, prod-go:1.26) with no prod-:latest tag, and a job-level container directive cannot resolve a concrete version inline, so the language-container route is a dead end. The uv concern that motivated the container was independently handled ~45 min later in setup/vergil (84bf315e, fd62605c), which now installs uv on bare runners.

Dropping the container restores the pre-regression bare-runner execution that passed CodeQL on 2026-05-27. The runner supplies every language toolchain autobuild needs; setup/vergil supplies uv for vrg-sarif-evaluate.

docs.title: CI
docs.text:
• add build-only docs verification to PR CI Add a reusable ci-docs.yml workflow that stages the docs the same way the CD docs deploy does and runs mkdocs build --strict — build only, no mike, no push, no credentials. Documentation that fails to build is now caught pre-merge as a CI gate instead of post-merge in the CD docs job.

Factor the changelog/release-notes staging and nav patching into a shared actions/shared/docs/stage composite action used by both ci-docs and cd/docs/deploy, so CI and CD build the docs identically and a green CI docs check predicts a green CD deploy. The deploy action no longer stages inline; cd-docs.yml runs the shared stage step before deploy.

The CI workflow self-guards on mkdocs config presence so repos without docs are unaffected, and is wired into this repo's own ci.yml on the default prod container for parity with the cd-docs deploy.

docs.title: Bug fixes
docs.text: • treat missing origin/main as a first-release no-op A repo with no origin/main is in a legitimate bootstrap / pre-release state: nothing ships without main, so there is no published version to diverge from. The fetch step previously ran 'git fetch origin main' unconditionally, which exits 128 (couldn't find remote ref main) and failed the whole version-bump job, permanently blocking PRs on repos whose only long-lived branch is develop. The gate now probes the remote with 'git ls-remote --exit-code': a genuinely absent main is treated as a first-release no-op (job goes green), while real fetch/network errors (any other non-zero exit) remain fatal so they are not masked. The compare step already tolerated an empty main version. Closes the hard-failure described in issue #672.

docs.title: Documentation
docs.text:
• add v2.0→v2.1 canary design (#679) Design for piloting the fleet-wide vergil 2.0→2.1 migration in vergil-actions as the lowest-risk, self-referential canary. Records the pin-driven cache mechanism, the two-line functional change, verification flow, risk surface, and the lockstep generalization that feeds the fleet playbook (vergil-tooling#1371).

  • revise v2.0→v2.1 canary design after pushback (#679) Pushback review surfaced four corrections: the version-divergence gate requires a VERSION bump (pin-only PR fails CI); a stale absolute action ref (standards-compliance setup/vergil@v2.0) must become @develop; acceptance splits into a CI gate and a CD gate because the PR never runs the release path where the 2.1 deltas live; and the doc scope includes the README @v2.0 consumer examples. Adds the two-version-axes explanation and folds the new lessons into the fleet generalization.

  • drop unneeded VERSION bump from canary design (#679) Verified origin/main=2.1.0 and develop=2.1.1, so a feature branch off develop already diverges from main and the version-divergence gate passes without a VERSION bump. Removes the erroneously-added VERSION change, returning the set to three changes (pin, standards-compliance ref, docs), and records the divergence-state check as the general rule.

  • expand canary doc scope to full @v2.0 sweep (#679) Discovered ~66 stale @v2.0 consumer references (11 in the workflows README, 55 across the published docs site) beyond the originally-scoped handful. Per decision, the canary does a full sweep of current consumer-facing refs to @v2.1, excluding historical records under docs/specs and docs/plans.

  • add v2.0→v2.1 canary implementation plan (#679) Task-by-task plan for the three-change set (tooling pin, standards-compliance @develop ref, full consumer-doc @v2.0 sweep), local validation gate, and PR/CI gate, with the CD gate and playbook implementation as follow-ups.

  • note no-auto-close-keyword PR constraint (#679) The standards-compliance check (vrg-pr-issue-linkage) rejects Closes/Fixes keywords, so migration PRs must link the issue without them. Captured in the CI-gate section and flagged as a per-repo playbook item; surfaced during alignment review of the implementation plan.

  • bump consumer @v2.0 references to v2.1 (#679) Sweep all current consumer-facing version refs onto the v2.1 line: CLAUDE.md host-install (v1.4 to v2.1), 11 refs in the workflows README, and 55 across the published docs site. Historical records under docs/specs and docs/plans are left as point-in-time records.
